prompt.context: Your client is a manufacturer of a revolutionary mattress that uses a new technology that promotes great nights of sleep. It's a small company run by the original inventor, who is fanatical about this technology. They currently have annual revenues of about $100M, selling in all kinds of retail stores.
prompt.question: They are now interested in entering the health care applications market, where this technology has been proven to alleviate the common problem of bed sores in the elderly and chronically ill. The inventor has hired Bain to help him determine whether or not to enter the health care market. Should the client enter the health care market?

clarifying_info.q: What segments of the health care market are we considering?
clarifying_info.a: We will look at hospitals as one pool and long-term care (LTC) as another.

clarifying_info.q: How many beds are in each segment?
clarifying_info.a: There are approximately 950,000 hospital beds and 1,700,000 LTC beds in the US.
Hospitals replace beds after 7 years; LTC facilities replace beds after 8 years.

clarifying_info.q: What portion of each market is the premium segment?
clarifying_info.a: The premium portion of the hospital market is 25%; in the LTC market it is only about 2%.

clarifying_info.q: What price would each segment pay?
clarifying_info.a: Hospitals would pay $500 per bed; LTC facilities would pay $300 per bed.

clarifying_info.q: What are the growth rates of each market?
clarifying_info.a: Hospitals are growing at 1% per year; LTC at 3% per year.
It is an extremely fragmented market.

clarifying_info.q: How do competitor products compare to ours?
clarifying_info.a: The client is positive that its product is superior.
Nearly all competitors are suppliers of a broad array of medical equipment and supplies.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current cost structure and price point?
clarifying_info.a: It costs $350 to manufacture a bed; current SG&A allocation is $100 per bed; each bed currently sells for $700–$750.

framework: Market size: estimate revenue potential across hospital and LTC segments (number of establishments × beds per establishment × replacement frequency × price)
Competitive space: number and concentration of current competitors, similarity of product offerings, breadth of competitor product lines
Cost of entry: manufacturing cost (presumably unchanged), distribution, sales force, and marketing required to access health care procurement channels

questions.prompt: How many beds per year are being purchased in the hospital market and the LTC market?
questions.guidance: Treat replacement as a continuous process: divide total beds by replacement cycle. Hospital: 950,000 / 7 ≈ 135,000 beds/year. LTC: 1,700,000 / 8 = 212,500 beds/year (can round to 215,000).

math.setup: Total beds ÷ replacement cycle = annual purchases

questions.prompt: How large is the addressable premium market in dollars for hospitals and LTC?
questions.guidance: Apply the premium share to annual beds purchased, then multiply by the relevant price point. Hospitals: 135,000 × 25% = 33,750 ≈ 35,000 premium beds × $500 = $17.5M. LTC: 212,500 × 2% = 4,250 ≈ 4,000 premium beds × $300 = $1.2M.

math.setup: Annual beds × premium share × price = market revenue

questions.prompt: Are the economics attractive given current cost structure?
questions.guidance: Current cost floor is $350 manufacturing + $100 SG&A = $450/bed (before any additional sales/marketing for a new channel). Hospital price of $500 yields only ~$50 gross margin per bed; LTC price of $300 is below even manufacturing cost. Entering a new market would likely raise SG&A above $100, making hospital margin near zero or negative and LTC clearly loss-making.

math.setup: Cost per bed vs. new-market price points
steps: Hospital price: $500 → margin = $50/bed (thin, before incremental sales/marketing)
math.answer: Hospital margin is razor-thin (~$50/bed, likely negative after incremental entry costs); LTC is structurally loss-making at $300 vs. $450 cost floor

brainstorming.prompt: What competitive dynamics or access challenges should concern the client about entering these health care segments?

categories.name: Product / vendor breadth
ideas: Competitors supply a broad array of medical equipment and supplies, giving them preferred-vendor status
Hospitals and LTC facilities prefer consolidating suppliers; a single-product vendor faces procurement barriers
Client's product is superior but that advantage may be insufficient to win contracts on merit alone

categories.name: Distribution and sales
ideas: Health care procurement differs significantly from retail; new sales force or channel partnerships required
GPOs (Group Purchasing Organizations) control much hospital buying; gaining GPO approval takes time and cost
LTC facilities are fragmented but often use buying groups similar to GPOs

categories.name: Market growth
ideas: Hospital market growing at only 1%/year — minimal organic tailwind
LTC growing at 3%/year with longer-term baby boomer upside, but starting from a very small base ($1.2M)
Neither growth rate justifies the cost and complexity of channel build-out

categories.name: Organizational fit
ideas: Client is led by a product-focused inventor; health care sales cycles are long and relationship-driven
Regulatory considerations (FDA, hospital certification) may add compliance burden
Distraction from core $100M retail business could be significant

categories.name: Pricing pressure
ideas: Health care budgets are cost-sensitive; premium pricing that works in retail may not translate
Reimbursement dynamics (Medicare/Medicaid) could cap what facilities are willing to pay

recommendation: Do not enter either the hospital or the LTC health care market at this time
Both markets are too small (combined <$19M addressable) relative to the client's $100M base, and price points are at or below the current cost floor, leaving no realistic path to profitability
risks: If the client does not enter, a well-funded competitor with a broad product line could capture the health care channel and eventually use that foothold to compete in retail
Baby boomer demographics could accelerate LTC growth beyond the current 3%, making the market more attractive in 5–10 years
next_steps: Revisit health care entry in 3–5 years as LTC market size grows with aging demographics
Explore other adjacent applications of the technology (e.g., hospitality, military, athletes) where pricing and channel economics are more favorable
If health care entry is still desired, consider a partnership or OEM arrangement with an existing broad-line medical supplier rather than building a direct sales force
